almond.habit: Medium-sized deciduous tree with a spreading habit.
almond.features: Serrated leaves; the first fruit tree to bloom in spring, often in February.
almond.flowers: Pale pink or white blossoms; fruit is a drupe with a leathery hull containing the nut.
almond.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; requires a long, hot summer to ripen nuts properly.
almond.care: Minimal pruning required; remove dead or diseased wood in summer. Water well during fruit swell.
facts: Botanically, almonds are not nuts, but 'drupes' (stone fruits) like peaches.
Almonds are entirely dependent on bees for pollination.

apple.habit: Deciduous tree, 2–6m depending on rootstock; rounded, spreading crown.
apple.features: Clouds of blossom in spring followed by ornamental and edible fruit; good autumn colour.
apple.flowers: Five-petalled white or pale pink blooms, April–May, richly fragrant and highly attractive to bees.
apple.conditions: Full sun; fertile, moist, well-drained soil; most varieties hardy to -20°C.
apple.care: Prune for shape and airflow in winter; thin heavy crops in June for better fruit size. Feed with sulphate of potash in late winter.
facts: Most apple varieties require a compatible pollinator partner nearby to set fruit reliably.
The UK has over 2,500 recorded apple varieties, many dating back several centuries.

autumncrocus.habit: Bulbous perennial; leaves appear in spring, flowers emerge leafless from bare ground in autumn.
autumncrocus.features: Produces goblet-shaped flowers in September–November when most other plants are fading; leaves die back by midsummer.
autumncrocus.flowers: Pale lilac-pink, goblet-shaped flowers, September–November; each corm can produce up to six blooms.
autumncrocus.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; well-drained soil; naturalises well in grass or under deciduous trees; fully hardy.
autumncrocus.care: Plant corms in late summer, 10cm deep. Allow foliage to die back naturally in spring. Divide congested clumps every few years.
facts: Despite being called 'autumn crocus', it is not related to true crocuses — it belongs to its own family, Colchicaceae.
All parts are highly toxic; colchicine extracted from the plant is used in gout treatment and cancer research.

baylaurel.habit: Evergreen tree or large shrub, 5–15m if unpruned; dense, broadly conical habit.
baylaurel.features: Glossy, aromatic, dark-green leaves year-round; responds well to clipping into formal shapes.
baylaurel.flowers: Small, creamy-yellow flowers in April–May, followed by black berries on female plants.
baylaurel.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; any well-drained soil; tolerates drought once established; hardy to -10°C.
baylaurel.care: Clip to shape in late spring and again in late summer. Use secateurs rather than shears to avoid browning cut leaves.
facts: Bay laurel is the original source of the victor's laurel wreath in ancient Greece and Rome.
The dried leaves are a classic culinary herb — a key ingredient in bouquet garni and essential to a good stock.

beech.habit: Large deciduous tree reaching 20–40m at maturity; broadly domed crown with smooth grey bark.
beech.features: Silky, pleated leaves emerge lime-green in spring; rich copper tones in autumn; persistent dry leaves on hedges through winter.
beech.flowers: Inconspicuous catkins in April–May; followed by triangular beech mast in papery husks.
beech.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; well-drained, chalky or sandy soil; dislikes waterlogging; very hardy.
beech.care: Little pruning needed as a tree. As a hedge, clip once in late summer to retain dead leaves through winter for privacy.
facts: Beech is known as the 'mother of the forest' — its dense canopy suppresses competing undergrowth.
Beech mast is edible and was historically ground into flour or pressed for oil in times of scarcity.

broom.habit: Deciduous shrub, 1–2m; upright, arching green stems with a wispy, open habit.
broom.features: Vivid yellow pea-flowers smother the bare green stems in late spring; architectural winter silhouette.
broom.flowers: Bright yellow, occasionally bicoloured, pea-like blooms, April–June; lightly fragrant.
broom.conditions: Full sun; poor, free-draining, acid to neutral soil; drought tolerant once established; hardy to -15°C.
broom.care: Cut back by two-thirds immediately after flowering to prevent woody legginess — never cut into old wood. Short-lived; replace every 10 years.
facts: The Plantagenet royal dynasty took its name from the Latin for broom, Planta genista.
Broom has nitrogen-fixing root nodules, making it a natural soil improver on poor ground.

buckthorn.habit: Deciduous large shrub or small tree, 3–6m; dense, twiggy habit with slightly spiny branches.
buckthorn.features: Provides excellent wildlife value — flowers for insects, berries for birds; attractive autumn leaf colour.
buckthorn.flowers: Small, yellow-green, four-petalled flowers in May–June; followed by glossy black berries in autumn.
buckthorn.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; tolerates most soils including chalk and clay; very hardy; good hedging plant.
buckthorn.care: Prune after berry season in late winter if needed. Excellent as part of a mixed native hedge.
facts: Buckthorn berries were historically used as a strong purgative — hence the species name 'cathartica'.
It is the sole foodplant of the Brimstone butterfly, one of the first butterflies seen each spring.

camellia.habit: Evergreen shrub or small tree; dense, rounded habit with glossy, leathery dark green leaves.
camellia.features: Provides structural greenery year-round; blooms during the bleakest months of late winter.
camellia.flowers: Rose-like blooms in white, pink, or red; appear February–April. Avoid early morning sun which burns frosted buds.
camellia.conditions: Partial shade; acidic, moist, well-drained soil (ericaceous); sheltered, west or north-facing aspect.
camellia.care: Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape. Feed with ericaceous fertilizer in spring and early summer.
facts: The tea we drink (Camellia sinensis) is a close relative of the ornamental camellia.
In the 19th century, they were the ultimate luxury flower, often worn in buttonholes of formal attire.

chamomile.habit: Low-growing annual or perennial herb; mat-forming with feathery, apple-scented foliage.
chamomile.features: Cheerful daisy-like flowers over a long season; the foliage releases a sweet apple fragrance when crushed.
chamomile.flowers: White ray petals around a raised yellow dome; June–September; attractive to hoverflies and small bees.
chamomile.conditions: Full sun; poor to moderately fertile, well-drained soil; drought tolerant once established; fully hardy.
chamomile.care: Deadhead to prolong flowering. Trim back after flowering. Non-flowering 'Treneague' variety makes a fragrant lawn.
facts: The ancient Egyptians dedicated chamomile to the sun god Ra and used it to treat fevers.
A chamomile lawn was planted at Buckingham Palace — chamomile releases its scent when walked upon.

cherry.habit: Deciduous tree, varying from compact dwarfs to large canopy trees.
cherry.features: Glossy bark with horizontal lenticels; vibrant autumn leaf colors.
cherry.flowers: Masses of white or pink blossoms in spring (April), followed by fleshy drupes in summer.
cherry.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; protect blossom from late frosts.
cherry.care: Prune only in summer (never winter) to prevent Silver Leaf disease. Protect fruit from birds.
facts: The cherry blossom (Sakura) is a symbol of renewal and the fleeting nature of life in Japan.
The word 'cherry' comes from the town of Cerasus in Turkey.

clematis.habit: Climbing perennial, 2–10m depending on variety; twines by leaf-stalk tendrils.
clematis.features: One of the most versatile garden climbers; vast range of flower size, colour, and season across the genus.
clematis.flowers: Saucer-shaped, star-shaped, or bell-shaped blooms in white, pink, purple, red, or yellow; season varies by group.
clematis.conditions: Head in sun, roots in shade; fertile, moist, well-drained soil enriched with compost; generally hardy to -15°C.
clematis.care: Pruning group determines timing: Group 1 (spring-flowering) — light tidy after flowering; Group 2 (large early) — light prune February; Group 3 (late-flowering) — cut hard to 30cm in February.
facts: Clematis is known as the 'Queen of Climbers' and has been cultivated in British gardens since the 16th century.
The silky seed heads of wild clematis, Clematis vitalba, gave rise to its common name 'Old Man's Beard'.

dandelion.habit: Herbaceous perennial with a deep taproot; forms a flat rosette of jagged leaves.
dandelion.features: One of the most important early-season food sources for pollinators; clock-like seedheads are iconic.
dandelion.flowers: Bright yellow composite flower heads, March–October; close at night and in dull weather.
dandelion.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; any soil; extremely hardy and adaptable.
dandelion.care: If grown deliberately, allow to flower freely for pollinators. Roots can be harvested and roasted as a coffee substitute.
facts: A single dandelion seedhead can carry up to 200 seeds, each capable of travelling miles on the wind.
Every part of the dandelion is edible — leaves in salads, flowers in wine, and roots as a herbal remedy.

elder.habit: Large deciduous shrub or small tree, 3–6m; upright, arching, with corky, furrowed bark.
elder.features: Two seasons of ornamental interest — foamy white flower plates in early summer, then heavy clusters of deep purple-black berries in autumn.
elder.flowers: Large, flat-topped corymbs of tiny, fragrant, creamy-white flowers; May–June; highly attractive to insects.
elder.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; tolerant of most soils including wet or chalky ground; very hardy.
elder.care: Prune hard in winter to control size, or leave as a specimen tree. Berries must be cooked before eating.
facts: Folklore warns that cutting down an elder without asking the 'Elder Mother' permission brings bad luck.
Every part of the plant is used: flowers for cordial and fritters, berries for wine and syrup, bark in folk medicine.

elderflower.habit: Large deciduous shrub or small tree; upright and arching with corky bark.
elderflower.features: Large pinnate leaves; provides wildlife value through flowers and later, berries.
elderflower.flowers: Large, flat, creamy-white 'plates' of tiny scented flowers; May–June.
elderflower.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; tolerant of most soils, including wet or chalky ground.
elderflower.care: Prune hard in winter if you need to control size. Can be treated as a hedge or a specimen tree.
facts: Folklore warns that cutting down an elder tree without permission from the 'Elder Mother' brings bad luck.
Every part of the plant is used: flowers for cordial, berries for wine, and wood for whistles.

fennel.habit: Tall, herbaceous perennial with a feathery, airy habit; up to 2m.
fennel.features: Fine, needle-like bronze or green foliage; smells strongly of aniseed.
fennel.flowers: Large, flat umbels of tiny yellow flowers in mid-to-late summer.
fennel.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; very deep taproot makes it drought-resistant.
fennel.care: Cut back dead stems in late winter. If you don't want seedlings, deadhead before seeds drop.
facts: In the Middle Ages, fennel was hung over doors on Midsummer's Eve to ward off evil spirits.
The town of Marathon in Greece gets its name from 'marathos', the Greek word for fennel.

fern.habit: Deciduous or semi-evergreen perennial; forms a shuttlecock of arching fronds, 60–120cm.
fern.features: Brings lush, architectural greenery to shaded spots; unfurling croziers in spring are ornamental in their own right.
fern.flowers: Non-flowering; reproduces by spores produced in sori (brown dots) on the undersides of fronds.
fern.conditions: Partial to full shade; moist, humus-rich soil; excellent under trees; fully hardy to -20°C.
fern.care: Remove old fronds in early spring before new growth emerges. Mulch annually to retain moisture.
facts: Ferns are among the oldest plant groups on earth, predating dinosaurs by over 200 million years.
Before their reproductive spores were understood, ferns were thought to have invisible seeds — gathering them on Midsummer's Eve was said to make you invisible.

fig.habit: Deciduous shrub or small tree; spreading habit with decorative silver-grey bark.
fig.features: Large, deeply lobed, architectural leaves; produces a milky sap when cut.
fig.flowers: Invisible (the 'fruit' is actually an inverted flower/syconium); fruits ripen in late summer.
fig.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil. Best with restricted roots (e.g., in a pot) to encourage fruiting.
fig.care: Prune in spring to remove crossing branches. Protect young fruits with fleece in severe winters.
facts: The fig tree is one of the first plants ever cultivated by humans.
In many cultures, the fig is a symbol of peace, fertility, and prosperity.

foxglove.habit: Upright, clump-forming biennial or short-lived perennial. Reaches 1–1.5m in height.
foxglove.features: Tall spires of bell-shaped flowers; soft, hairy, mid-green basal rosettes in the first year.
foxglove.flowers: Tubular, nodding bells in shades of purple, pink, or white with spotted throats, May–July.
foxglove.conditions: Partial shade to full sun; prefers moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; hardy to -20°C.
foxglove.care: Deadhead spent flower spikes to encourage a second flush or leave for self-seeding. Cut back to ground in autumn.
facts: Source of digitalin, used in heart medication, but the plant is highly toxic if ingested.
Folklore suggests foxes wore the flowers on their paws to silence their movements while hunting.

fuchsia.habit: Deciduous shrub, 60cm–2m; arching branches with a graceful, pendulous habit.
fuchsia.features: Produces its distinctive dangling bicoloured blooms prolifically from midsummer to first frost.
fuchsia.flowers: Pendant two-toned flowers with reflexed sepals and a contrasting corolla, typically red and purple; June–October.
fuchsia.conditions: Partial shade to full sun; moist, fertile, well-drained soil; hardier varieties to -10°C; tender types need frost-free overwinter.
fuchsia.care: Hardy varieties: cut back to healthy buds in April once frost risk has passed. Tender varieties: lift and store frost-free or take cuttings in September.
facts: Named after the 16th-century German botanist Leonhart Fuchs by Charles Plumier, who first described the genus.
Fuchsia berries are edible and slightly sweet — they were eaten by the Māori people of New Zealand.

gardenmint.habit: Vigorous, spreading herbaceous perennial; upright stems 30–90cm, spreading by underground stolons.
gardenmint.features: Bright, spearmint-scented foliage; one of the most useful culinary herbs in the kitchen garden.
gardenmint.flowers: Whorls of tiny lilac-pink flowers on tapering spikes, June–September; excellent for bees and butterflies.
gardenmint.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; moist, fertile soil; best grown in a container to prevent invasive spread.
gardenmint.care: Pinch out flower buds to keep foliage production going. Cut hard after flowering for a flush of fresh leaves.
facts: Spearmint gets its name from its spear-shaped leaves, and has been used as a breath freshener since Roman times.
Ancient Greeks rubbed mint on their arms before athletic competition, believing it increased strength.

grape.habit: Vigorous deciduous woody climber; uses tendrils to scale supports up to 10m+.
grape.features: Large, lobed leaves with beautiful autumn tints of yellow or red.
grape.flowers: Inconspicuous green flowers in spring, followed by clusters of edible berries.
grape.conditions: Full sun; deep, well-drained soil; needs a warm, sheltered spot to ripen fruit.
grape.care: Prune in early winter (while dormant) to prevent 'bleeding'. Thin fruit bunches in summer for better quality.
facts: Vitis vinifera has been cultivated for over 8,000 years, beginning in the Caucasus region.
A single grapevine can produce enough grapes for 40 to 60 glasses of wine.

grapevine.habit: Vigorous deciduous woody climber; uses tendrils to scale supports up to 10m+.
grapevine.features: Large, lobed leaves with beautiful autumn colour; can clothe walls, pergolas, and arches magnificently.
grapevine.flowers: Inconspicuous green flowers in spring, followed by bunches of edible or ornamental fruit in late summer.
grapevine.conditions: Full sun; deep, well-drained soil; needs a warm, sheltered spot to ripen fruit reliably in the UK.
grapevine.care: Prune in early winter while dormant to prevent excessive 'bleeding'. Thin fruit bunches in summer for quality.
facts: Vitis vinifera has been cultivated for over 8,000 years, beginning in the Caucasus region.
A single grapevine can produce enough grapes for 40 to 60 glasses of wine.

hollyhock.habit: Tall biennial or short-lived perennial; upright, architectural stems reaching 1.5–2.5m.
hollyhock.features: Classic cottage garden plant; stately vertical spikes of saucer-shaped flowers are a midsummer icon.
hollyhock.flowers: Large, tissue-paper flowers in shades of white, pink, red, purple, or near-black; June–September.
hollyhock.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; sheltered from strong winds to prevent stem damage; hardy to -15°C.
hollyhock.care: Stake tall varieties. Remove flowering stems after blooming to encourage perennial behaviour. Prone to rust — remove affected leaves promptly.
facts: Hollyhocks were brought to Britain from the Holy Land by Crusaders — 'holy' plus 'hoc' (mallow) gives its name.
Hollyhock flowers are edible and were used to add colour to wine in the Middle Ages.

hop.habit: Vigorous climbing herbaceous perennial; twining bines grow up to 6m in a single season.
hop.features: Bold, lobed, bright-green leaves create excellent rapid seasonal cover; papery cone-like flowers are highly decorative.
hop.flowers: Female plants produce pale green, cone-like strobiles (hops) in August–September; wonderfully ornamental when dried.
hop.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; requires strong support; fully hardy to -20°C.
hop.care: Cut all growth to the ground in autumn. Train new bines up supports in spring. Golden-leafed 'Aureus' variety is less vigorous.
facts: Hops have been used to flavour and preserve beer since the 9th century.
The hop plant is related to cannabis and nettles — all members of the family Cannabaceae.

hydrangea.habit: Deciduous shrub with a rounded, bushy habit; typically 1–2m tall.
hydrangea.features: Large, ovate, serrated leaves; attractive dried flower heads provide winter interest.
hydrangea.flowers: Large mopheads or lacecaps in blue, pink, or white; July–October.
hydrangea.conditions: Partial shade; moist, well-drained soil. Soil pH affects color (acid for blue, alkaline for pink).
hydrangea.care: Prune in spring, cutting back old flower heads to just above a pair of strong buds.
facts: The name comes from Greek 'hydor' (water) and 'angos' (vessel), referring to its water-loving nature.
In Japan, hydrangeas are associated with heartfelt emotion and apologies.

iris.habit: Herbaceous perennial with a creeping rhizomatous habit; sword-like fans of grey-green foliage.
iris.features: Architectural foliage provides vertical interest; striking 'bearded' flower structure.
iris.flowers: Exotic three-petaled blooms with 'falls' and 'standards' in almost every color; peaks May–June.
iris.conditions: Full sun (rhizomes need baking); neutral to lime-rich, well-drained soil; very hardy.
iris.care: Divide rhizomes every 3-4 years after flowering. Trim leaves to a fan shape in autumn to prevent wind rock.
facts: Named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow, Iris, who acted as a messenger between heaven and earth.
The 'Fleur-de-lis' symbol of French royalty is a stylized representation of the iris.

jasmine.habit: Vigorous deciduous twining climber, 4–10m; slender, scrambling stems.
jasmine.features: Few plants can match the intensity of its fragrance on warm summer evenings; fast-growing wall cover.
jasmine.flowers: Small, starry white blooms in loose clusters, June–September; one of the most powerfully scented of all garden plants.
jasmine.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; fertile, well-drained soil; sheltered from cold winds; hardy to -15°C.
jasmine.care: After flowering, thin out old and congested stems to maintain airflow and encourage new growth. Tie in new shoots regularly.
facts: Jasmine oil is one of the most expensive in perfumery — flowers must be hand-picked before dawn when fragrance is strongest.
In many cultures jasmine symbolises love and beauty; it is the national flower of Pakistan and the Philippines.

juniper.habit: Evergreen coniferous shrub or small tree; hugely variable in form from prostrate to columnar.
juniper.features: Provides year-round structural interest; attractive silver-blue berries persist through winter; one of only three native UK conifers.
juniper.flowers: Inconspicuous yellow male cones in spring; female plants produce round green berries that ripen to blue-black over two to three years.
juniper.conditions: Full sun; any well-drained soil including chalk and poor ground; very hardy to -30°C.
juniper.care: Requires little pruning. Remove dead or diseased wood as needed. Extremely drought-tolerant once established.
facts: Juniper berries are the defining botanical flavour of gin — they are not true berries but fleshy seed cones.
Juniper wood was burned in Scottish folk tradition to protect against evil spirits and disease.

laurel.habit: Evergreen tree or large shrub, 5–15m if unpruned; dense, broadly conical habit.
laurel.features: Glossy, aromatic, dark-green leaves year-round; responds well to clipping into formal shapes.
laurel.flowers: Small, creamy-yellow flowers in April–May, followed by black berries on female plants.
laurel.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; any well-drained soil; tolerates drought once established; hardy to -10°C.
laurel.care: Clip to shape in late spring and again in late summer. Use secateurs rather than shears to avoid browning cut leaves.
facts: Bay laurel is the original source of the victor's laurel wreath in ancient Greece and Rome.
The dried leaves are a classic culinary herb — a key ingredient in bouquet garni and essential to a good stock.

lavender.features: Silver-grey aromatic foliage year-round; provides structure in winter.
lavender.flowers: Violet-blue to pale lilac spikes, June–August; highly attractive to bees.
lavender.conditions: Full sun, excellent drainage, alkaline to neutral soil; extremely drought tolerant.
lavender.care: Cut back to new growth in April; avoid cutting into old wood. Trim spent flowers in late summer.
facts: Name from Latin 'lavare' — to wash; used by Romans to scent bathwater.
Roman soldiers carried it for its wound-healing properties.

lemon.habit: Small evergreen tree or spreading shrub; often grown in containers in temperate zones.
lemon.features: Glossy green leaves; fragrant white flowers; can have sharp thorns.
lemon.flowers: Small, waxy white flowers with a heavy citrus scent; can flower and fruit year-round.
lemon.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, slightly acidic soil; needs minimum 10°C in winter.
lemon.care: Move indoors or to a conservatory in winter. Feed with specialized citrus fertilizer. Avoid overwatering.
facts: A single lemon tree can produce up to 600 pounds of lemons in a year.
During the Renaissance, lemons were used as a cosmetic to redden lips and as a cleaning agent.

lemonbalm.habit: Bushy herbaceous perennial, 60–90cm; forms a dense clump of lemon-scented foliage.
lemonbalm.features: Intensely lemon-scented leaves useful fresh or dried; excellent bee plant; easy to grow.
lemonbalm.flowers: Small, two-lipped, white to pale yellow flowers in whorls along the stems, June–September; highly attractive to bees.
lemonbalm.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; any moderately fertile, well-drained soil; fully hardy to -20°C.
lemonbalm.care: Cut back hard after flowering to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh foliage. Divide in spring or autumn.
facts: Melissa is the Greek word for bee — lemon balm was rubbed inside hives to encourage swarms to settle.
Lemon balm has been used as a calming herbal remedy since at least the 14th century.

lilyofthevalley.habit: Low-growing rhizomatous perennial, 15–25cm; spreads steadily by underground runners to form colonies.
lilyofthevalley.features: Broad, arching, deep-green leaves; dainty arching stems of pendant white bells in late spring.
lilyofthevalley.flowers: Tiny, pure white, bell-shaped, intensely fragrant flowers on arching stems, April–May.
lilyofthevalley.conditions: Partial to full shade; moist, humus-rich soil; excellent under deciduous trees; fully hardy to -20°C.
lilyofthevalley.care: Leave largely undisturbed once established — it resents root disturbance. Divide congested clumps in autumn to rejuvenate.
facts: Lily of the valley is the traditional flower for May Day and was one of the flowers in Princess Kate's royal wedding bouquet.
All parts of the plant are highly toxic, despite its delicate appearance and heavenly scent.

limetree.habit: Large deciduous tree, 20–40m; broadly columnar with a rounded crown; vigorous suckering at base.
limetree.features: Heart-shaped leaves cast deep shade; fragrant midsummer blossom is beloved by bees; excellent avenue tree.
limetree.flowers: Small, pale yellow, intensely fragrant flowers in pendant clusters, June–July; a magnet for bees.
limetree.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soil; very hardy to -25°C.
limetree.care: Remove basal suckers regularly as they appear. If pollarding or pleaching, prune in late winter before growth begins.
facts: The linden or lime tree was sacred in Germanic and Slavic traditions — village meetings were held beneath them for centuries.
Dried lime blossom makes a calming herbal tea (tilleul) that remains popular across continental Europe.

magnolia.habit: Deciduous or evergreen tree/shrub; often spreading and architectural with smooth grey bark.
magnolia.features: Fuzzy, velvet-like flower buds in winter; large, dramatic leaves follow the spring bloom.
magnolia.flowers: Large star-shaped or tulip-shaped blooms in white, pink, or purple; March–May before leaves appear.
magnolia.conditions: Full sun or dappled shade; neutral to acidic soil; sheltered from cold winds to protect flowers.
magnolia.care: Minimal pruning required; remove crossing or dead branches in mid-summer. Mulch annually in spring.
facts: Magnolias are among the most ancient flowering plants, existing before bees (they are pollinated by beetles).
The flower represents dignity and perseverance due to its ability to survive for millennia.

marigold.habit: Hardy annual, 30–60cm; branching, slightly sticky, aromatic stems with a bushy habit.
marigold.features: One of the easiest and longest-flowering annuals; cheerful orange and yellow daisy flowers from spring to frost.
marigold.flowers: Single or double daisy-like blooms in shades of orange, yellow, and cream, April–October if deadheaded regularly.
marigold.conditions: Full sun; any well-drained soil, including poor soils; very hardy as seedlings; self-seeds freely.
marigold.care: Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering over many months. Sow direct in March–April or September for early flowers the following year.
facts: Calendula petals are edible and have been used to colour butter and cheese since medieval times.
A companion planting favourite — marigolds deter whitefly and attract beneficial hoverflies to the vegetable garden.

marshmallow.habit: Tall herbaceous perennial, 1–2m; upright, branching stems with soft, velvety, grey-green leaves.
marshmallow.features: Elegant cottage garden plant with soft, downy foliage and a long flowering season; deeply rooted and drought tolerant.
marshmallow.flowers: Pale pink, five-petalled mallow flowers, 3–4cm across, in the upper leaf axils; June–August.
marshmallow.conditions: Full sun; moist, deep soil — tolerates wet or salty conditions; excellent for coastal gardens; fully hardy.
marshmallow.care: Cut back to ground level in autumn. Self-seeds gently — allow a few seedlings to replace ageing plants.
facts: The original marshmallow confection was made from the mucilaginous root of this plant mixed with sugar.
The roots have been used medicinally for over 2,000 years to soothe sore throats and digestive complaints.

mint.habit: Vigorous, invasive herbaceous perennial spreading via underground runners.
mint.features: Square stems and serrated, highly aromatic bright green leaves.
mint.flowers: Spikes of tiny lilac flowers in late summer; loved by pollinators.
mint.conditions: Partial shade to full sun; prefers moist, fertile soil.
mint.care: Best grown in a pot to contain its spread. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh leaves.
facts: In Greek myth, Minthe was a nymph turned into the plant by Persephone out of jealousy.
There are over 600 varieties of mint, including chocolate, pineapple, and ginger mint.

oleander.habit: Vigorous evergreen shrub or small tree; upright and mounding to 2–4m.
oleander.features: Narrow, leathery, willow-like dark green leaves; drought and salt tolerant.
oleander.flowers: Funnel-shaped blooms in clusters of white, pink, red, or apricot; June–September.
oleander.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; very heat tolerant; hardy to -5°C (needs winter protection in cold zones).
oleander.care: Prune in late winter to maintain shape. Wear gloves as all parts are highly toxic.
facts: One of the most poisonous commonly grown garden plants; even the smoke from burning it is toxic.
It is the official flower of the city of Hiroshima, as it was the first to bloom after the 1945 bombing.

olive.habit: Evergreen tree or shrub with a slow-growing, architectural habit.
olive.features: Narrow, silvery-grey leaves; beautiful gnarled trunks on older specimens.
olive.flowers: Tiny creamy flowers in summer, followed by green olives that ripen to black.
olive.conditions: Full sun; very well-drained soil; very drought tolerant; hardy to approx -10°C.
olive.care: Prune in spring to thin out the center. Feed in spring. Can be kept in pots for many years.
facts: Olive trees are incredibly long-lived; some specimens in the Mediterranean are over 2,000 years old.
The olive branch has been a symbol of peace and victory since ancient times.

peony.habit: Bushy herbaceous perennial or woody shrub (Tree Peony); long-lived and substantial.
peony.features: Deeply divided dark green foliage; new shoots emerge as striking deep red 'noses' in spring.
peony.flowers: Large, often fragrant, bowl-shaped flowers in white, pink, or crimson; peaks May–June.
peony.conditions: Full sun to dappled shade; deep, fertile, moist but well-drained soil; hardy and reliable.
peony.care: Provide support for heavy flower heads in spring. Cut back herbaceous types to ground level in autumn.
facts: Peonies can live for over 100 years if left undisturbed in the right conditions.
In Chinese culture, it is known as the 'King of Flowers' and symbolizes honor and wealth.

peppermint.habit: Vigorous herbaceous perennial, 30–90cm; spreading by underground stolons.
peppermint.features: Strongly aromatic dark green or purple-tinged leaves; one of the most cooling and recognisable of all herb garden scents.
peppermint.flowers: Dense, blunt spikes of tiny lilac-pink flowers, July–September; highly attractive to bees and butterflies.
peppermint.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; moist, fertile soil; best grown in a pot to contain spreading habit; fully hardy.
peppermint.care: Cut hard after flowering for a second flush of fresh leaves. Replace plants every 3–4 years as they lose vigour.
facts: Peppermint is a natural hybrid between water mint and spearmint, first described in England in 1696.
The world's largest peppermint oil producer is the Willamette Valley in Oregon, USA.

poppy.habit: Annual (field poppy) or clump-forming perennial (oriental poppy); upright, bristly stems 60–90cm.
poppy.features: Tissue-paper petals of extraordinary translucent colour; dramatic seedheads are highly ornamental when dried.
poppy.flowers: Large, bowl-shaped blooms in red, orange, pink, white, or purple with a dark basal blotch, May–July.
poppy.conditions: Full sun; poor to moderately fertile, well-drained soil; annual species self-seeds prolifically; fully hardy.
poppy.care: Annual: scatter seed in autumn or early spring directly where they are to flower — they dislike transplanting. Perennial: cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh basal foliage.
facts: The red field poppy became an enduring symbol of remembrance for the fallen of World War One.
Poppy seeds can remain viable in soil for over 100 years, germinating when the ground is disturbed.

quince.habit: Small deciduous tree with a twisted, characterful trunk and branches.
quince.features: Large, pale pink blossoms; golden, highly fragrant, pear-shaped fruit in autumn.
quince.flowers: Attractive single pink/white flowers in May; fruit is covered in a fine grey fuzz when young.
quince.conditions: Full sun; moist but well-drained soil; prefers a spot near water but not waterlogged.
quince.care: Prune in winter to maintain an open center. Harvest fruit as late as possible before frost.
facts: Quinces are so aromatic they were used as room deodorizers in the Victorian era.
In ancient Greece, the quince was given at weddings as a symbol of fertility.

raspberry.habit: Deciduous suckering shrub with upright, usually prickly stems (canes).
raspberry.features: Divided leaves, white beneath; fruit is an aggregate of drupelets.
raspberry.flowers: Small, white, drooping flowers in late spring/early summer.
raspberry.conditions: Full sun (but tolerates some shade); rich, slightly acidic, moist but well-drained soil.
raspberry.care: Summer-fruiting: prune flowered canes to ground in autumn. Autumn-fruiting: prune all canes to ground in February.
facts: Unlike many fruits, raspberries do not continue to ripen after they are picked.
The 'fruit' is actually a cluster of tiny individual fruits, each containing a seed.

rhubarb.habit: Vigorous herbaceous perennial, 60–90cm; large, crinkled leaves on long, fleshy, colourful stalks.
rhubarb.features: Bold architectural foliage makes a statement in the kitchen garden; one of the first edible crops of the year.
rhubarb.flowers: Tall, creamy-white flower plumes in June — remove promptly to redirect energy into the stalks.
rhubarb.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; deep, fertile, well-manured soil; tolerates heavy clay; fully hardy to -20°C.
rhubarb.care: Force early crops by covering crowns with a pot or bucket in January. Never harvest in the first year; take no more than half the stalks in subsequent years.
facts: Rhubarb leaves are highly toxic due to oxalic acid — only the stalks are edible.
The 'Rhubarb Triangle' between Wakefield, Morley, and Rothwell once produced 90% of the world's forced rhubarb.

rose.habit: Diverse; including climbers, ramblers, shrubs, and miniatures; deciduous woody stems.
rose.features: Pinnate leaves with stipules; stems often armed with prickles (thorns).
rose.flowers: Varying from single (5 petals) to fully double; highly fragrant; peaks June, often repeats until frost.
rose.conditions: Full sun; heavy, fertile, well-drained soil; benefits from mulching.
rose.care: Prune in late winter (February/March). Feed in spring and mid-summer. Deadhead regularly.
facts: Roses are one of the oldest species of plants, with fossils dating back 35 million years.
The rose hip (fruit) of some species contains more Vitamin C than any other fruit or vegetable.

rosemary.habit: Woody evergreen shrub; can be upright (to 1.5m) or prostrate/trailing.
rosemary.features: Needle-like aromatic leaves, dark green above and white-felted beneath.
rosemary.flowers: Small, two-lipped flowers in pale blue or white; often blooms in early spring and autumn.
rosemary.conditions: Full sun; sharply drained soil; sheltered from cold, drying winds.
rosemary.care: Prune after flowering to prevent legginess. Propagate from semi-ripe cuttings in summer.
facts: Long associated with memory; students in ancient Greece wore rosemary garlands while taking exams.
In folklore, it is said that where rosemary flourishes, the mistress of the house is the master.

sage.habit: Evergreen sub-shrub with a bushy, spreading habit; 60cm x 60cm.
sage.features: Textured, pebbly, grey-green leaves; highly aromatic and soft to the touch.
sage.flowers: Spikes of bluish-purple flowers in early summer.
sage.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, even sandy soil; very drought tolerant once established.
sage.care: Prune lightly in spring. Do not prune in autumn as new growth may be damaged by frost.
facts: The name 'Salvia' comes from the Latin 'salvere', meaning 'to be saved' or 'to heal'.
Ancient Romans used it as a digestive aid and a memory enhancer.

sourcherry.habit: Small deciduous tree or large shrub, 3–5m; suckering habit with a spreading crown.
sourcherry.features: Masses of white blossom in spring; bright red, slightly tart cherries in summer; excellent wall-trained specimen.
sourcherry.flowers: White, five-petalled blossom in clusters, April–May; a superb early source of nectar for bees.
sourcherry.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; fertile, well-drained soil; one of the few fruit trees that crops reliably on a north-facing wall.
sourcherry.care: Prune after fruiting in summer — never in winter — to prevent Silver Leaf disease. Net against birds.
facts: Sour cherries self-fertilise, unlike sweet cherries which need a pollination partner.
The Morello cherry, a variety of sour cherry, has been grown in British gardens since the 17th century.

sunflower.habit: Fast-growing annual herb; can reach 1m to 4m depending on variety.
sunflower.features: Tall, thick hairy stems with large, heart-shaped, rough leaves.
sunflower.flowers: Large composite heads with yellow ray florets and dark central discs; July–September.
sunflower.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, fertile soil; requires plenty of water during growth.
sunflower.care: Sow in April. Stake tall varieties. Leave heads in autumn for birds or harvest seeds.
facts: Sunflowers display heliotropism, turning their heads to follow the sun across the sky.
A single sunflower can contain up to 2,000 seeds.

thyme.habit: Low-growing, woody evergreen sub-shrub or carpeting groundcover.
thyme.features: Tiny, highly aromatic grey-green leaves; drought-tolerant and rugged.
thyme.flowers: Clusters of tiny tubular white to pale purple flowers; June–August.
thyme.conditions: Full sun; poor, gritty, very well-drained soil; hates winter wet.
thyme.care: Lightly trim after flowering to keep it compact. Replace plants every 3-5 years as they go woody.
facts: In ancient Greece, thyme was a symbol of courage; soldiers would bathe in thyme water before battle.
It is a primary source of thymol, a powerful natural antiseptic.

tulip.habit: Spring-flowering bulbous perennial; upright stems ranging from 10cm to 70cm.
tulip.features: Broad, glaucous green leaves; sleek, symmetrical goblet-shaped blooms.
tulip.flowers: Vast range of colors (except true blue) and forms (lily-flowered, parrot, fringed); April–May.
tulip.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; benefits from a sheltered spot to prevent wind damage.
tulip.care: Plant bulbs deep (3x height) in late autumn (November) to avoid 'Tulip Fire' fungus. Deadhead after flowering.
facts: In 17th-century Holland, 'Tulip Mania' caused bulb prices to exceed the cost of a house.
Tulip petals are edible and can be used in salads, though bulbs are toxic.

valerian.habit: Tall, upright herbaceous perennial; reaching 1m to 1.5m.
valerian.features: Pinnate, deeply toothed foliage; fern-like appearance at the base.
valerian.flowers: Small, scented pale pink or white flowers in dense terminal clusters; June–August.
valerian.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; prefers moist, heavy soils; very hardy.
valerian.care: Cut back after flowering to prevent self-seeding. Divide in spring or autumn.
facts: The root has been used since ancient times as a sedative and sleep aid.
Cats are often as attracted to valerian as they are to catnip.

wildpansy.habit: Annual or short-lived perennial; low, spreading or slightly climbing, 10–45cm.
wildpansy.features: Charming, old-fashioned flowers with distinctive 'faces'; an ancestor of the cultivated garden pansy.
wildpansy.flowers: Small tricoloured flowers in combinations of purple, yellow, and white, with darker veining; April–September.
wildpansy.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; well-drained to moderately moist soil; self-seeds freely; fully hardy.
wildpansy.care: Allow to self-seed for a naturalistic effect. Deadhead to prolong flowering if preferred.
facts: Also known as 'heartsease', it has been a symbol of love and remembrance since medieval times.
Shakespeare references it in A Midsummer Night's Dream as the magic flower used by Oberon.

wildthyme.habit: Prostrate, mat-forming evergreen sub-shrub; creeping stems, 2–10cm tall.
wildthyme.features: Forms a fragrant, flowering carpet that tolerates light foot traffic; ideal for cracks in paving or dry banks.
wildthyme.flowers: Masses of tiny, tubular pink-purple flowers covering the plant, May–August; one of the best plants for bees.
wildthyme.conditions: Full sun; poor, gritty, sharply drained soil; tolerates drought; fully hardy to -20°C.
wildthyme.care: Trim lightly after flowering to keep compact. Propagate from cuttings or by dividing rooted stems.
facts: Wild thyme was believed to be a resting place for fairies in English folklore.
The ancient Greeks burned thyme as incense in their temples, and 'thymos' may relate to the Greek word for courage.

wisteria.habit: Vigorous deciduous woody climber; requires strong support for its twining woody stems.
wisteria.features: Pinnate green leaves that turn yellow in autumn; impressive, gnarled trunks as the plant ages.
wisteria.flowers: Long, drooping racemes (up to 30cm) of fragrant, pea-like mauve or white flowers; May–June.
wisteria.conditions: Full sun for best flowering; fertile, moist, well-drained soil; south or west-facing walls.
wisteria.care: Prune twice yearly: in summer (July/August) cut long shoots to 5-6 buds; in winter (January) cut to 2-3 buds.
facts: Wisteria can take up to 20 years to flower if grown from seed; always buy grafted plants.
A single wisteria plant in Sierra Madre, California, is known as the 'largest blossoming plant in the world'.

wormwood.habit: Semi-evergreen perennial sub-shrub; upright, mounding habit, 60–90cm.
wormwood.features: Intensely aromatic, silver-grey, finely divided foliage is among the most beautiful of any garden plant.
wormwood.flowers: Small, unremarkable yellow-grey button flowers in late summer; the foliage is the real ornamental feature.
wormwood.conditions: Full sun; poor, very well-drained, even dry soil; drought tolerant; fully hardy.
wormwood.care: Cut back hard in spring to prevent woodiness and maintain a compact silver mound. Avoid wet, heavy soils.
facts: Wormwood is the key botanical flavouring in absinthe, the notorious 19th-century liqueur.
The active compound thujone gives it a powerful bitterness that has been used to repel moths and parasitic worms for centuries.
